div.head: Scene
div.stage: “Justice Touchit, Frank, and Freeman, discovered seated at table, as drinking their Wine after Dinner, (noise and laughter).

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: “BRAVO! Bravo!”

sp.speaker: Free.
sp.p: “Leave Justice Touchit alone, when a pretty girl is in question. My old school fellow, though purblind at all other times, is then as quick-sighted as the youngest amongst us.”

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: “I bring you in there before the Court, neighbour; you never come into company, but you must bring a petticoat with you.”

sp.speaker: Free.
sp.p: “I!—Nay, I declare, gentlemen—”

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: “Why, have not you always one in your head, neighbour?”

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: “Bravo!—the Justice again!—Fine the culprit.”

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: “Give him first a glass of wine, and then let us have the good old glee he sung so well last night; that honest pipe of his shall finish the present sitting; and then all to our afternoon's business. Come, neighbour, fill and sing.”

sp.speaker: Free.
sp.p: “With all my heart.”

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Well, master Frank, now that we are alone, let us change the discourse, and attend to your story.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: I'faith, Mr. Justice, there ben't much need o' change, for what I had to tell you; because, to zay the truth, it's all one as what we ha' been talking of.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Eh! how, you young rogue! what, you have made some poor girl miserable, and now you're come to me, because I've been an old friend of the family, to get you out of the scrape!

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Noa, noa, Mr. Justice, you be on the wrong scent; you mistakes me down right.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Eh! do I? well, what is it, then? unfold.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: You remember my little zister Phœbe!

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Ay, do I, a nice little ruddy, round, comfortable—

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Yes, as to the matter o'that, the girl was well enough.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Zounds! well enough? why she was enough to rouse the blood of an old, sober, prudent, reserved, phlegmatick fellow, like myself.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Well, well, a man might go farther, and fare worse, sure enough; but that's nothing to the purpose now, Mr. Justice.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Well, aye, as you say, to the purpose— what of Phœbe, little Phœbe, Eh!

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: She's a ruinated girl.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Oh, Lord! Oh, Lord! I hope not.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Too true—lost.—

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Lost!—and who is the thief?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: One 'Squire Zingle.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Single!

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Aye, Peregrine Zingle, Esquire.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Single!—Peregrine Single, a very odd name.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: He came to our town from some outlandish place beyond sea, and speaks but a sort of half English; but our Phœbe says, he comes of a family in Cornwall; and what's main-strange, was one of three at a birth.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Ah, that's more odd still.—Three Singles! very odd.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: They were the wonder of the county, and be nick-named the Three Peaze, 'cause they were all alike the zame as one another; and, if they had worn the zame clothes, you could not know which is which, Mr. Justice.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Not know which is which!

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Their father be dead o' late, and, as the story goes, ha' left them plenty to pay for mourning.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Three Singles!—very odd—And, so, Mr. Peregrine took a liking to Phœbe!—well, and what is the proof of all this mischief?—a baby, eh?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: No, not so bad as that, neither.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: No! what, then?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Why, I'll tell you, Mr. Justice. You must know as how, one day last autumn, whilst I was in Lancashire, where I do go every year—

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Aye, no matter.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Comes this young spark to our house, and finds Phœbe alone in her room.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Oh, Lord! alone in her bed-chamber!

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: No, I don't say bed-room, but her own room, where she sits of a day.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Oh! well.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: There they were, close shut up together for upwards of an hour.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Well? well?—and is that all? Why, there might be no harm in that, honest Frank.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Aye, but our maid Dolly peep'd thro' the key-hole, and zee'd 'em.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Eh!—hold!—Eh!—what!— your maid Dolly look'd thro' the key-hole, and saw—Eh!—well, well, what did she see?—tell me all in order.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Why, first, she 'zeed 'Squire Zingle kiss our Phœbe's hand.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Eh! did he? I warrant you, those little round dimpled fingers were as soft as sattin.—Well, and then?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Well, and then she 'zeed him kiss her lips.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Eh!—oh, the rogue! to touch those pouting, cherry—Oh, Lord!—well, and then?—

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: And then—I be almost ashamed to tell you, master Touchit.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Oh, don't mind me, I'm a justice, you know, I am used to these things.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: And then she 'zeed him put his arm round her waist.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Waist! a plague on't, he'd be puzzled to do that. Women have no waist, now-a-days. Well, well, and what then?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: And then Dolly open'd the door, and run'd into the room.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Oh, Lord! Oh, Lord! that was very unlucky—I mean, that was very lucky indeed.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: I know'd no more of these goings on than a blind buzzard, till I com'd home just after the 'Squire is gone away; so i'fags, I zet out after him; and I warrant I'll be up with him, go as fast as he will.— I'll soon let him zee he ha' got the wrong sow by the ear.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Well, but friend Frank,—

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Don't you say a word for him, master Touchit: zooner than I'd zee our Phœbe fool'd in this way, I'll swinge he and all his brothers one after another, if there were fifty of them.—I know what's to be done;—only, passing by your house, I thought, for old acquaintance sake, to ask a bit of advice.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Master Frank, I would not have you be too much in a hurry on this matter—these are difficult points, and require proof.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Ay, ay, I've got proof enough—I know it's all true,—I know what's right; I only comes for advice.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Well, well, but, my good friend, you must not be so hasty.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: I ben't hasty, Master Touchit, I ben't hasty.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Well, that's right; I'd have you speak to him, and say to him—

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: You need not tell I that, Master Touchit; I knows what to say to him, I only comes for a bit of advice.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: But, zounds! you won't take my advice.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Yes, yes, that's what I comes for, but, Master Touchit, you won't give me the kind of advice that I do want. I want, do you see, that sort of advice that a man expects from a friend, when he ha' made up his mind.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Why, faith, that's not an uncommon way of asking advice, now-a-days. Well, then, I'd have you ask him as many questions as you please, in your civil, polite way.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Yes, yes, I can talk like a gentleman. I inherits the genteel thing from father. What's bred in the bone will never go out of the flesh.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: That's right again, I'd have you behave genteely, Frank, on all occasions.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Just as I intends; that's good advice, now— Just what I had made up my mind to—that's just what I came to ask you for. Thank ye, kindly, Master Touchit.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Well, I wish every one was as easily satisfied in what he asks for.—You'll remember to be genteel.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Oh, I be famous, I tell ye, for a bit of gentility.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Aye, Aye, you give a sample of it.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: The Names of Daffodil, Hydra, and Moon, written over three Doors, which lead to different apartments.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Nay, Humphrey, this inn seems a very good one.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Yes, yes, I think it will do very well for us.
And there seems to be a nice little sort of a body yonder.— Yes, I think we may stay here.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Do you look to every thing, Humphrey; I can attend to nothing at present.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: No, Sir! I cannot comprehend that, any way in the world; a gentleman to come up all this way to fetch his bride, that is to be, and to be so cast down!—Don't trouble yourself, any way in the world, about it, sir; leave it all to me.—I'll give them notice in the country—I'll take care of the preparations. Bless us! what a rare holiday this wedding will make in our house!

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: And yet, Humphrey, I could be melancholy on such an important change of my life.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: How fine it will look in all the newspapers! in the Sun, and the Moon, and the Post, and the Star, and the Telescrap, and the Sunday Monster, and all the flying Mercuries!

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Aye, my name, too, where most I dread to see it, in a newspaper!

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: We must, Sir, we must be mentioned among the births and marriages in the Gazitt.— Yesterday was married Pertinax Single. Esquire, a gentleman of good qualities—that's you, sir—and a good estate in Cornwall, and master of that good, excellent, domestick, Humphrey Grizzle—that's me—to Miss Emily Milford, a young lady possess'd of every accomplishment to make the marriage state happy.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: So report says, Humphrey.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: And we shall say so, I don't doubt, Sir, when we see her.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: You know it is merely in compliance with a parent's anxious desires, in his last moments, that I pay this visit to Miss Milford.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: We have talk'd of all that before, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Now, Humphrey, in order to investigate her character and disposition thoroughly, before I make proposals, I intend to use a little artifice, in which you must be careful not betray me.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Oh, don't be afraid of me, any way in the world, Sir.—It is a proper match.—It will do us credit.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Aye, if my scheme succeed. I shall, to day, carry Miss Milford a letter, which introduces me to her only as a friend of mine. Under that disguise I shall be able to learn her inclinations towards me.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: She cannot dislike us, be assur'd, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: But if I should not like her!—she may have a hundred good points, and not one to suit me.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: 'Tis hard to chuse, Sir. If a man has an ugly wife, whom nobody likes, it is a bit of the Devil; and, if he has a handsome one, whom every body falls in love with, then that's the Devil himself. It's best to take them blindfold.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: My father had a high opinion of Miss Milford, and—

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: And I'm sure, when we wrote to ask leave to make proposals, she sent us a very agreeable answer.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Aye, rather too readily; she may be a very pretty girl, that's something, to be sure; but, from her consenting to accept proposals from a man she had never seen, I am afraid she may have a coarse mind, and that won't do for me.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: No, that won't do for us any way in the world.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: However, this stratagem will enable me to act with the utmost circumspection.—I wish the first interview were over.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: You won't expect us to be very sober at your wedding, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: A good servant should share the joy of his master; and on that occasion, Humphrey, I give you leave to get drunk every day, if that's your pleasure.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Oh! fie, Sir! get drunk every day!

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: What objection have you?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Can't do it, Sir, any way in the world— It is impossible, you know, to get drunk every day, unless one is first sober every day.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Well then, I won't expect you to return to your senses for a week.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: That's short allowance—you don't think to come to your senses again so soon, Sir, do you?— Oh, what an appearance we shall make at church!

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: I'fackins, who'd have thought I should have found him so soon l There stands Squire Peregrine, as unconcern'd now, as if his conscience were right and tight; but mayhap, he hav'nt got a conscience— There be some folk without one.—Zarvant, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Your servant, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: I'd speak a few words with you, if you please.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: If you please, Sir, what may your business be with me?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Pray, Sir ben't your name Zingle?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: The same, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: May I make so bold to ask if you don't call yourself a gentleman?—
Let's see what he'll say to that!

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: I hope I do not claim that name without deserving it.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: May be—
Now I'll at him at once. —Pray, Sir, do you know one Phœbe Woodbine?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Phœbe! Phœbe Woodbine?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Pray, Sir, do you hold yourself bound, as a gentleman, to speak the truth?
There I has him.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Most unquestionably.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: I be a bad hand at a long parlaver, and so I'll be glad if you'll answer me in a few words, on your truth, as a gentleman, whether you ever wrong'd my zister Phœbe Woodbine?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: To answer in the same laconic stile, I never did.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Will you give me your word?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: I give you my word and honour.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: That's enough—you gives me your word and honour as a gentleman—I am satisfied—The Justice advised I so. Egad, if you had wrong'd her, Measter Zingle, I'd have spoil'd some of the tailor's work about you.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Now, pray, Sir, give me leave to enquire your name.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: My name?—No no, come, that's too bad.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Upon my word—

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Aye, aye, I takes your word, and that's enough; let's leave while it is well—I don't want to make you drink other than you brew.—So now I think I've shew'd him a bit of my politeness, I'll be off home again, and talk a little kind to our Phœbe. —Zarvant, Squire.—Now I think I leaves him like a gentleman.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Why surely this man must be mad, to talk to me of having wrong'd his sister.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Lord, Sir, have you done such a wicked thing?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: You blockhead! why you are mad too!

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: I don't know, Sir—We are so near our wedding, that—

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: A truce with your jests, Humphrey.— This is the room, I think, they shew'd us, is it not?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Yes, Sir,
The Hy—Hy—dra—Yes, that's our room. Sir.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: I'll just take a look at it, then proceed to Mr. Milford's, house, and if they are not at home, leave the letter I told you of.—Go you, Humphrey, to the Post-Office, and see if my letters are arriv'd—I order'd my attorney to send me an exact statement of my possessions and revenues, for Miss Milford's inspection. When a woman is going to sacrifice her liberty, she ought, at least, to know what she is to have in exchange for it.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Yes, we may as well go to the Post-Office; I dare say there'll be a letter for one of us.

sp.speaker: Waiter.
sp.p: Coming—coming—

div.stage: [First Waiter crosses the stage, and goes out.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Hark'ye, which is the way to the Post-Office?

sp.speaker: Second Waiter
sp.p: This way—this way—if you please—Its hard by—

div.stage: [Humphrey goes out with Second Waiter on the side opposite to that at which he entered with his master Pertinax.
[The First Waiter re-enters with Renard carrying a trunk, marked with the name of Peregrine Single, in large brass letters.

sp.speaker: First Waiter.
sp.p: This way, Sir, this way, if you please.

sp.speaker: Ren.
sp.p: Allons! ou etes vous donc?—Ca, prenez, quick, shew my master de room—quick, he will not lose de time.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Renard!

sp.speaker: Ren.
sp.p: Ici, Monsieur. Quick!—Here is Mr. Peregrine himself.

div.stage: [Second Waiter carries the trunk into the Daffodil and Exit.
Renard going out, meets Peregrine, who enters dress'd in a great coat, and singing.

sp.speaker: Ren.
sp.p: Bien chanté, a merveillé!

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Is the room ready, fellow?

sp.speaker: First Waiter.
sp.p: This way, if you please, Sir, this is your room, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Ah, diable! these heavy English roads!

sp.speaker: Ren.
sp.p: Ah, oui, Monsieur, noting like de beau pavé of France.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Help me off with my great coat. Ah! there—

div.stage: [First Waiter carries the great coat into the Daffodil, and then Exit.

sp.speaker: Ren.
sp.p: Ah, ha! tres bien! charmant! ah! you quite forget de littel girl now—little pretty Phœbe, eh? n'est il pas vrai?

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: No, I cannot get her quite out of my head yet.

sp.speaker: Ren.
sp.p: Pas encore?

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: I am afraid I am in love.

sp.speaker: Ren.
sp.p: Amoureux! Est il possible?

sp.speaker: Pereg,
sp.p: Possible! yes, it is possible! but I'll try your receipt for it, Renard.—gaiety and variety, that's the cure, eh?

sp.speaker: Ren.
sp.p: Oui, Monsieur, gaieté, varieté, and de dance, dat is de vay my nation do.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Give me my foils—this is a fine hall for fencing.

sp.speaker: Ren.
sp.p: Oui, tres belle salle.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: I'll take a lunge or two, perhaps that may do me good.

sp.speaker: Ren.
sp.p: Oui, oui, dat is de way—you must jump de here, and dance de there, and sing and fence.— Let de littel girls get into your heart!—Oh, si donc!

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Ah, very true, Renard, 'tis a sottise.

sp.speaker: Ren.
sp.p: Assurement, tres grand sottise—de littel girls, dey be pour les Messieurs pour se divertir—for the gentlemen deir pastime, dat is all; when you go away, you never tink any more of dem. Alerte! you tink of de little Phœbe dis last month,—now you think of somebody else.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Ma foi, very true, Renard, you are an excellent maitre and philosophe, tres habile upon my honour.—D'ye think I shall get Phœbe out of my head, then?

sp.speaker: Ren.
sp.p: You take my advice, Monsieur, you voiager; you go see de ball, de theatre, and de pretty ladies here; to-morrow morning, j'engage, you shall not tink any more of littel Phœbe.—Alerte, Monsieur, prenez—
sp.stage: [Gives Peregrine the foil, fences with him.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Parbleu! I feel the good effects of your advice already—I begin to be quite moi-meme again—
—A plague of the girls, when they once get into one's thoughts, there's an end of all farther accomplishments—
—Ay, ay, this will do.

sp.speaker: Ren.
sp.p: Ah, ha! yes, dat is de way—oui, ma foi, je suis tres habile—yes, dat is very true. Nous autres Francois, we are all de most clever people in de whole world,—and we do not keep it a secret —point de reserve en cela; begar, we tell it ourselves. —I shall write my life,—Vie de Renard, written par soi-meme, by his own myself.—“Ce será la plus belle chose!”

div.stage: Enter Pertinax from his room, crossing the stage.

sp.speaker: Pert.
sp.p: Yes, I will call at Miss Milford's. By disguising my name, I shall have opportunities of discovering her disposition, and shall secure an easy retreat in case she disappoints my expectations. Nothing can be more alarming than to take a leap into matrimony without first surveying the ground.

div.stage: Enter Humphrey, from the opposite side of the Stage. with two letters in his hand.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: For— Single, Esq.—No Christian name! from the lawyer! Humph! I never before knew a lawyer use a word too little.
For Humphrey Grizzle! why not Esq.? There's a word too little there too. This attorney must have very little practice.
Well, let's read that over, and then I'll take the other to my master.
Oh, here he is—Where the devil did he get that great hat?—I don't remember that in our trunk. —This is for you, Sir,

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: And this is for you
Parry, carte, segond, tierce, ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Lord, Sir, what are you at?

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: If my adversary were not quick, I should have surpris'd him there.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Quick! egad, you'd surprise the quick and the dead too!

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Retire—lunge—no, that's wrong.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Wrong! why your head is wrong, I believe.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: I'll go through an attack regularly

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: This is a sudden attack indeed!

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Was it not? no touching without being quick.—Quick—quick!

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Well, I have been quick. You told me to fetch our letters immediately, and here they are, one for me, and one for you.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: I know nothing about you—Ecartez vous —out of my way, for when I am in the heat of practice, I would as soon run a man through the body as look at him.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Upon my word, Sir, since you have been going to be married—

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: I going to be married, rascal! I'll cut your throat in earnest, if you say such a thing.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: It's too late to deny it—you must be married, we can't be off now.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: I'll try that; in the mean time, tenez for your impertinence
sp.stage: (beats Humphrey with the foil, and returns fencing, into the Daffodil.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Oh, lud! that's not our room. Why you are gone into the wrong room, Sir!

He's going mad! The sight of marriage certainly alters us. What a pretty figure we should make in that case, when we go back to our house in the country? Half the senses we brought out between us, the lesser half clean gone!

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: A man in affairs of love, I find, has no great talent for recollection.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: In truth I think so.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Who would have thought of my calling on Emily just at the very hour, when I was told that no one here is to be found at home! However, I left the letter of introduction; so half the business is done. Oh, Humphrey, have you got my letters?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: I've got your marks at least—Have you left off fencing, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Fencing!

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: He seems pretty quiet again—Pray, Sir, how do you find yourself?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: What do you mean, Humphrey?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Do you perceive any hardness about the eyes, any swimming in the head, or any—

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Oh, what you think I must be affected as my marriage draws nearer. Pho! pho! that was only a joke.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: A joke? No such jokes for me; I don't like jokes,
I'll not let him have his letters yet, to revenge myself.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: You do not answer, if you have got my letters?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Lord, Sir, what should make you think I have got them?
Now, if I had a mind, I suppose I might have another beating by way of joke. I have not got them, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Did not I send you for them just now?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Do you recollect that, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: To be sure.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: And do you recollect, Sir, that I offer'd them to you, and you gave me a thrust in the ribs in return, and told me not to interrupt you while you was at your carts, and parrises, and your ha! ha's! and sa! sa's? and did not you threaten to run me through the body? and did not you
beat me, by way of joke? What have you done with the swords, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Humphrey, I am sorry to perceive that you abuse the innocent liberty I allow you. Instead of executing my messages, you have been, I suppose, making free in the cellar.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: I, in the cellar! Upon my soul, Sir, saving your presence, it seems to me as if you had been there.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: You are drunk, Humphrey.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: I wish I was, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: I will not pardon such a neglect a second time. I am afraid you are not in a state, at present, to comprehend me.—You are very drunk.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Not in a state to comprehend him! I remember, when I had my fortune told me, I was bid to take care of my brains. Egad, it must certainly be so;
I'm going—I certainly am going;—then the greater half is lost. This comes of our wedding.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: No, it won't do, I won't stay alone; ha! ha!
Who is this fellow, I find here still?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Ah! I'm so chang'd he does not know me.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: The moment I sit down, pop, she comes into my head again.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: His head? Why then, 'tis his brains, and not mine. Egad, very likely; for after all, 'tis he who is to be married, and it is not my head that is in danger.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: What was that letter you brought me just now, fellow?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: So, he comes to himself by degrees.— Now he recollects that I offer'd it to him. Well, then, I may as well—
sp.stage: (pulling the letter by degrees from his pocket)

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.stage: (putting himself in an attitude of fencing)
sp.p: Come, Sir, be quick.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: No, I don't think it is quite safe to give it him yet.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Ha! ha!
Diable! I cannot get her out of my head. Ho! Renard!

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Yes, I see how it is—There is something in the sight of that letter, which affects him—I'll not shew it him again till he is out of danger of making jokes.

div.stage: Pertinax appears at the door of the Hydra.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Humphrey!

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Sir.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: It is strange no letters should arrive for me.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: What, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Try if you can find your way once more to the Post-office, and ask for them. If I am not at home here, bring them to Mr. Milford's.

div.stage: [Exit into the Hydra, shutting the door.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: There! now he has forgot again that I brought him the letter. Poor gentleman! he seems to have chang'd his condition before marriage.—ha! ha! ha!—perhaps he has been taking a cup to drown his melancholy—though I never knew him in liquor —he leaves that to me.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Nothing but Phœbe, Phœbe!—nothing else in my head.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Phœbe, Phœbe, in his head! That must certainly be it, and this Phœbe is some new kind of cordial.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Nothing but Phœbe.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Pray, Sir, what kind of spirit is Phebe?

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Spirit! a divine spirit! a living angel!— Have you seen my rascal?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Your rascal, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Come along, Sirrah, you shall shew me the town, the public breakfast room, the walks, the theatres, the—

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Lord, Sir! you had better stay, Sir, till you are a little—a little—
—I never saw him in his cups before.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: What is the fool making those grimaces for?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: The fool! he is far gone sure enough, to call me a fool.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Blockhead! why don't you set forward?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Why, Sir, do you forget the post?

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Not while you stand before me—March! I say, March!

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Lead! on! I'm resolv'd on a turn up the town— A round after dinner—what greater delight?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: You had better by far let your bed be turn'd down; Or what will you think of the Round-house at night?

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: D'ye know what you're saying? He's tipsy, no doubt.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: I'll be seen by the town, so, sirrah, turn out!

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: You'll be seen by the town—Lud! what will turn out!

div.head: Scene

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: HUR cannot shew you petter rooms than these rooms, only that they are too quiet and too far from companies

sp.speaker: Mac.
Taff.
sp.p: Hur is not the mistress, but hur is the maid of the mistress.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: 'Cause you must know I have a young gentleman under my care, who wants a little furniture in the upper story

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: 'Splut! hur cannot shew the upper story; hur sleeps there hurself, and there is no furniture there, at all.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: Body and blood o'me, child, cannot, you take a plain speech into your understanding?

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Hur cannot understand you.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: Oh! fire and faggots, have I been a teacher of grammar and all the other seven sciences, and cannot explain my meaning to a simple country wench? Hark'ye, my dear creature, my name is Mac Floggen, and I have a young gentleman under my care, Mr. Percival Single, a very good gentleman, but he has not quite so sharp a set of wits as myself and his fellow creatures.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Oh, a little simple or so,

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: There now, mercy o' me, you've hit upon it souse at once. The case is this, there were three brothers all at one birth, what you may call three twins, and when nature is so over abundant, d'ye see, it is no wonder if she be a little deficient. My ward, Mr. Percival, was the youngest of the three twins who were born all at the same time.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Cot's plessings on the man! how can one be younger than the other, if they were all born at once?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: They were not all born at once, my dear, only at the same time. The two others, as I have heard, are two very sensible gentlemen, and run away with the learning of the family. Poor Mr. Percival! if it was not for my instructions, he'd scarce be able to speak common English.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Ah! that would be creat pities.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: And so as I don't like to expose the poor gentleman, I keep him as much as I can within doors by himself, while we are abroad together.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Goot, goot, hur will take care of him as long as you please to stay here.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: And that won't be long, faith—We are now but on our road to Bath, while we are stopping here. We pass'd two nights in the mail coach yesterday, by the way of the New Passage, and to-day, we have travelled the remainder of our journey, all but what is left of it. Odso, here is my dear pupil.

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: Uncle, uncle!

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: The dear simpleton always calls me so.

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: Lack-a-dazy, uncle, what a fine house!
sp.stage: [looking at Taffline, appears in admiration of her.]

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: This is not a house, my dear boy, 'tis an inn, where we shall hire lodgings to eat and dress and sleep in, while we are walking about in the pretty fields all day long.
He is a simple Solomon, so I explain every thing and make it all clear to him, you see.

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: And, uncle, uncle!

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: What do you say, Mr. Percival?

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: Shall we hire this fine lady, too?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: Ah, he is always thinking of hiring all the pretty girls that come in our way; you know I have told you, my dear boy, that when you are old enough to claim according to your grand papa's will and testament, you shall have a wife all to yourself, to keep your company when you're alone; but you must not take the married estate into your head, 'till you are old enough to come under the head of the estate that is left you in tail. That's what I call explaining the matter clearly to him; you see.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Cot's plessings! he is prave wits to understand you.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: I'll take a small look at the apartments. Keep your eyes upon Mr. Percival, that he may not get out of your sight, and don't leave him alone, unless there be somebody else with him.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Hur will stay here and take care you shall have no troubles and fears.

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: How handsome you are!

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! he will grow very fond of hur in a moment, Sir.

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: Oh, dear! how civil she is! I wanted to ask you a question,—
Do you love me? Tell me your name, it must be a pretty one.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Hur likes you very indifferent well, Sir, and hur name is Taffline, at your service. Poor fool! what should hur see to love in him?

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: I am very rich, I have got money in my purse; look here.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: That's not much like a fool neither! What will you do with all your monies?

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: I'll give it all to you.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Hur likes him a little petter.

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: If you will love me and let me kiss you.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Ot's plessings, hur cannot let any gentleman kiss hur here in the hall.

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: I will tho'—but then you must not tell uncle, he'll be monstrous angry, he is so cross.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Indeed! on your conscience?

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: Oh, he is indeed, indeed; because he is such an ugly old man, the pretty girls don't like him;— now they like me vastly.

sp.speaker: Mac Floggen
sp.p: —Where are you, my dear boy, where are you?

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: Oh dear, here he is—don't tell him what I said about him.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: No, not a word, depend on hur.

div.stage: Enter Mac Floggen from the Moon.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: Come, my dear boy, these rooms will suit us to a hair; you may go into them immediately.

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: Shall not this fine lady shew us the way, uncle?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: No, no, she has something else to attend to—
Let your mistress know we shall stay here, and as to the price of the apartments, tell her we'll have no words about that,—but I'll explain it all by talking to her myself.

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.stage: [looking at Taffline as he goes into the Room]
sp.p: —Heigho!

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Cot pless hur, he is a prave young gentleman. If it pleases Cot of his grace to mend his fancies, hur can like him very well.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: So, here's a pretty piece of work! all the credit of our house gone at once! my master is gone out of his wits, and I must go out of the family! I that used to conduct my master so properly. can't keep him in order now, any way in the world. —Dragging me all about the town, and talking nonsense to all the girls in the street! He that was so shy and so sheepish, he could hardly look a lady in the face! wanted me to lend my arm too, to one of his minxes! I won't bear it; I'll discharge him; he shan't live with me; he shall not be my master any longer; he does not deserve such a gentleman-like domestic—No; I'll get rid of his letter, and then I'll get rid of him.

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: I wish I could find that handsome lady again. Hollo!

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Sir!

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: I say, I wish you would desire that handsome lady to come again.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Why, what the devil is he at? He was mad before, then drunk, and now simple!—What lady do you want?—I shan't bring you any ladies, indeed.

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: Don't you know where Taffline is?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: What, the Welch chamber-maid? So! in doors, and out of doors, it's all the same game.— Here, here's your letter.

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: Oh! a letter is of no use to me; I have never learn'd my letters. But I tell you what—if you'll go and fetch that pretty lady, Taffline, here, I'll give you this purse
sp.stage: (holds out a purse to Humphrey, who stands surprised).
sp.p: Ah! I must go and look for her myself. I can't get an answer from you. It's my belief you are foolish. I never saw such a simpleton in all my life, ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Foolish! a simpleton?—
I certainly must be dreaming! If I could meet somebody that knows me, I would enquire whether I am awake or not—
Hark ye, Taffline

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Hur is in creat hurries; what is the gentleman please to want?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Do I see you?

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: If you is coote eye sights, hur is not very far off.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Do you know me?

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: You are one of the companies in the house; hur knows as much of you as of all the others.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Are my eyes open or shut?

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Why, sure, the man is foolish, to ask such a questions.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Foolish! why, he said I was foolish!— Taffline, I have great reason to believe I am asleep; do bite my finger, that I may know whether I am asleep or not.
Hollo! Hollo! what the devil are you at?

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Did not you bid hur to pite your finger?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Yes; but I didn't bid hur to pite it off!

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Ah! hur was in too creat hurries to pite any more gently.
Hur cannot stay now, to hear your prate. There is so much companies in the house, hur cannot run up stairs and down stairs fast enough for every body.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: No, I am not asleep, that's certain: then it must be either my brains or my master's are slipped out of doors: I'll follow him, and see what other people think of us. I'll try if he will refuse to take his letter before company.—Oh, Lord! Oh, Lord! what would I give to know whether it is me or my master that is crazy.

sp.speaker: Mr. M.
sp.p: No, my dear girl; you may guess the feelings of a parent on such an occasion. Old Single was my particular friend; but I have not seen his sons since they were lads at school. Pertinax was always my favourite; Peregrine was too volatile and conceited; and Percival was a mere simpleton. I should like Pertinax for a son-in-law; but I should be loth to influence your opinion.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: The proposal from Mr. Pertinax was sudden and unexpected; and therefore to whom should I apply for advice, but to a kind and tender parent?

sp.speaker: Mr. M.
sp.p: My advice, Emily, is, that you should chuse for yourself: see him first: all I can say on his side, is, that if young Pertinax make but as good a husband as old Pertinax, a girl cannot meet with better fortune.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: The gentleman, madam, who left a letter here this morning, is below.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: Desire the gentleman to walk up.
Now for the account of my lover's sudden change of health, or fancy: it is difficult to determine which.

sp.speaker: Mr. M.
sp.p: Well, I leave you to receive him, Emily, that you may make what enquiries you please, without restraint.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: I took the liberty
to call this morning, madam, and left a letter from Mr.— from my friend, Mr.—

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: Mr. Single, I believe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Yes, ma'am, from Mr. Single, ma'am—
Her appearance answers my wishes. I will observe what effect the letter has had.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: He speaks of you, Sir, as his most intimate friend, and excuses himself on the score of indisposition.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: I am his most intimate friend, Madam—
She might be a little more interested about my illness. I dare say she'd think no more of my death than of the drowning a blind puppy.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: His illness is not dangerous, I hope, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Come, that's something better.— He is exceedingly ill at present, madam; very ill, I assure you; very ill
at ease, I am certain.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: Real illness will not lessen the interest of a deserving man in my heart.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: How ingenuous! I see I shall run no risque in declaring myself.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: And though I am resolved never to sacrifice my liberty to a man whom I dislike,—

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Madam!—I beg your pardon, Madam— Dislike!—Do you dislike my friend, Mr. Single?—
There, now, that's prejudice. I'm sure she's quite a coquette.—Have you heard any thing, Madam, that—

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: By no means, Sir. The character which Mr. Single bears, has impress'd me with a favourable opinion of him; but, though his heart be good, his manners may not be pleasing.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Very true, ma'am.—
There's certainly a delicacy in that thought; and yet she agreed to receive my proposals without seeing me—there was an indelicacy in that—yet there's a softness and sensibility in her features!

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: Every trifle may be of importance. If you will not be too severe on female curiosity, I would take the liberty to ask you a few questions concerning him.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: As many as you please, ma'am.—
Oh, Lord! here's a scrutiny of all my good and bad qualities!—So! the tables are prettily turn'd upon me!

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: First, what sort of a looking man is he?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: What sort of a looking man, ma'am?
What the devil shall I say of my own looks?
My friend, Single, Madam, is—about my height—straight—not remarkably handsome—rather a plain kind of man.—To say the truth, ma'am, I never look'd at him very nicely.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: Well, Sir, person is the last consideration.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: That delicate confession is worth an empire.—I begin to love her already.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: Next, Sir, do you think him likely to be jealous?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Why, ma'am, I have, at times, known him so.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: Has he, then, been so often in love?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Ma'am, I!—I!—

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: The question, Sir, seems to embarrass you; if fickleness be a part of his character, I own I could not sacrifice myself to a man who would be likely to sacrifice me for the first new face he might admire.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Never! never!
So! I had nearly betray'd myself. This is the very woman, whose hand I would desire to receive at the altar. I wish the parson was in the room.—No, lovely Emily—
—the charms of your person, the readiness of your wit, your manners, your eyes—

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: Sir!—this behaviour and language!—

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Were only proofs of my zeal for my friend; nothing else, I assure you, madam.—Let me plead in excuse for my behaviour—

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: Your excuse, Sir, will he better made to my father, who is here.

sp.speaker: Mr. M.
sp.p: Hey day! what's all this about? excuses! I hope, Sir, nothing—How's this, my dear?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: So, I shall be kick'd down stairs as my own rival!

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: This gentleman's great regard for his friend, Mr. Pertinax, render'd his expressions a little too particular; but, as you are here, Sir, I beg no further notice my be taken of it.

sp.speaker: Mr. M.
sp.p: There is a servant below, with a letter, I believe, for you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: The direction will discover me.— Will you allow him to come up?

sp.speaker: Mr. M.
sp.p: I have ordered him up.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: You are very obliging.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Well, Humphrey, what news of your master?
Now, be careful, Humphrey, that you don't betray me.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: I betray you!

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: You recollect what I charged you with this morning at the hotel.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Yes, yes, I remember well enough what you charged me with; but I won't say a word about it.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: I have treated you as you deserve, Humphrey, and I expect no less in return.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Oh, I'll return it you whenever you please. Take your letter.—So! I'm glad I've got rid of that at last.
sp.stage: (Pertinax takes the letter, returns to Mr. Milford, and retires up the stage)
sp.p: he seems mighty quiet again! I hope the fit don't seize him before company.—
—She'll do—she'll do rarely for us.—Your servant, Ma'am

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: You are Mr. Single's servant, I believe.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: And your's, that is to be, Ma'am.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: Hey day! what is it all settled, then?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: All settled, Ma'am!—that is entirely my business—my master don't interfere in these things.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: Surely, your master must be of a very easy disposition.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: The best in the world, Ma'am. I take upon me to say
that my master, Mr. Pertinax, is one of the most accomplished, most pleasantest, good temper'd, good looking gentleman, in all Christendom.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Peace! you stupid—

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: You see, I do not betray you.— I won't say a word about the girls.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: I hope, Humphrey, your master is quite recovered.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Ma'am!—recovered!—
Oh, I suppose he was subject to these fits formerly, before we liv'd together.—Yes, madam, quite recover'd.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: His illness was very short.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: The fits come and go in a moment, a sort of intermitting disorder—
I understand you, Sir— I never saw any symptoms of it, madam, till we came here.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Stupid fellow! your master is not here.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Lord, Sir! how can you say so?—every body knows we came together.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: A plague of this fellow's dullness—What, your master?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Aye, Sir, I and you.—Oh, Lord! I have discover'd all!

sp.speaker: Em. and Mr. M.
sp.p: You, Sir!—are you Mr. Pertinax Single?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: It is no longer in my power to deny it:— I am that unfortunate man, who has unintentionally offended you—and the only amends I can make is to retire immediately.—Madam, your most obedient.

sp.speaker: Mr. M.
sp.p: Hold, Sir, a moment, if you please.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Not for the world—I know when I am troublesome. I am fully sensible of my indiscretion; therefore, you will permit me to—Sir, your most obedient.

sp.speaker: Mr. M.
sp.p: Nay, I am sure, Emily will be very willing to—

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Your pardon, Sir. No, it is impossible that a young lady of that extreme delicacy of mind which Miss Milford has shewn—you will excuse me; I can only beg ten thousand pardons, madam.—I beg, ma'am—I hope, ma'am—Madam, your most obedient

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: Stay, Sir.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Stay, Sir; don't you hear the lady bid us stay, Sir?

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: Suffer me, Sir, to ask you wherefore you came under this pretence to see me?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: From an apprehension, madam, that if my own inclinations did not second my father's wishes, I might render his ashes partakers of a crime in making you unhappy.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: The delicacy of this motive, Sir, requires no apology.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Lord, Ma'am! my master has none of these faults that he pretended: they do not belong to either of us.

sp.speaker: Pertinax.
sp.p: I am so happy and so ashamed, that I am at a loss how to express myself. My intentions, I believe, will be best proved by this letter, which Humphrey has just brought me from my attorney.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Yes, it comes from our attorney.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: It contains the particulars of my estate. Permit me, Sir, to put it into your hands.

sp.speaker: Mr. M.
sp.p: On no account: I could not think of offering you such an affront.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: You would hurt me extremely by refusing it. I consider the solemn engagements of matrimony of such importance, as to require the most explicit confidence on all sides.

sp.speaker: Mr. M.
sp.p: Well, sir, to satisfy you—but, really, it is rather on your account than mine.
“My dear Fellow,”

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Very familiar in our attorney!

sp.speaker: Mr. M.
sp.p: “The little girl whom you amused yourself with in this town, is run away, and is said to be in search of you. If you wish to avoid her, take your measures accordingly. Your old comrade in mischief,Bobby Breakwindows.”

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Burn our attorney!

sp.speaker: Mr. M.
sp.p: Is this, Sir, your confidence in me? Is this your respect for—

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: I assure you, Sir, that is not the letter which—

sp.speaker: Mr. M.
sp.p: This is the letter you put into my hands.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: That's very true

sp.speaker: Mr. M.
sp.p: I am really at a loss, Mr. Pertinax, what to say to you. If it was not for my regard for your father, I shou'd suppose you the most harden'd libertine that—

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: No, upon my soul, Sir, that's not my character.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: No, upon my soul, that's not our character.

sp.speaker: Mr. M.
sp.p: Your behaviour, Sir, is unworthy of any notice but this. Come, Emily, let us leave the room together.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: I am thunderstruck?—Is not this the letter you brought me, Humphrey?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Yes, yes; I've reason enough to know the looks of it. I wish I had kept it in my pocket, still. You had better have taken it before, when we were alone.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Blockhead! you never brought it to me before.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Oh, Lord! this is worse than your dancing and fencing.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: My dancing and fencing!

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Worse than your crying for the chambermaid.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Out of my sight.—Is this a time for your silly jests, when I am half distracted? what shall I do? At all events, this house is not the place for me. Come, sirrah, let us be gone; and, d'ye hear, no more of your silly jokes.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Let that be the bargain, if you please, Sir: I'll make none, if you promise to make none.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Come along, I say.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Stay, Sir!—How could you employ an attorney with such a cursed unlucky name, as Bobby Breakwindows.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Bobby Breakwindows!

div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE.—A View of the Hills near Cheltenham.

sp.speaker: Phœbe.
sp.p: Surely, I heard them following me!—No, 'twas a shepherd driving his flock across the field. What a fearful journey have I made! I take every noise I hear for the voice of some one pursuing me; and every leaf that shakes in the wind, for a robber. Would I could have overtaken my sweet Peregrine! It is impossible he can have forsaken me. I can scarcely believe that he has left me. Were I to indulge my fancy, I could dwell for ever on the happy moments we have pass'd together.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Wounds! ben't that our Phœbe?—

So, Phœbe—well found—a pretty tramping thee hast cost me—what ha' brought thee hither? Come, speak the truth— Odd, dang it, Phœbe, I be glad I ha' met thee again. If there wern't some good reason for it, thou would'st not have come all this way after 'Squire Peregrine.

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: I own it, Frank, I could not rest without striving to learn the reason of his leaving me so suddenly. I am afraid he must have met with some great misfortune.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Fie, you silly wench, he have more likely met with a great fortune.

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: Oh! I should be glad of that for his sake.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: I zeed him here at the great inn, hard by.

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: Here! Oh, Frank!

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Aye; and his servant told me afterwards he was come to take his wife, that is to be, down with him to his own house.

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: His wife!—Oh!

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Why, aye, what's the matter now?—Why, Phœbe!

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: His wife!—Oh, Frank!
he promised to make me his wife.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Did he?—Odds heart; did he?—Now, Master Touchit, what's come of a fine gentleman's word now? when he told me, as how, the straight forward contrary! Come, Phœbe, don't mind him. Odd, hang him! forget him, there's a good girl.
Oh, if I do but ever meet him again!

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: I will try to forget him—I will, indeed, Frank; but do not be so angry with me for loving him.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: There's a good girl, Phœbe; don't mind it—leave him to me—I'll make him repent it, never fear.

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: Oh, dear Frank, you look terribly angry.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Don't you mind, I—I'll—

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: You won't fight him, I hope, Frank.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: That's nothing to you, if I should.

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: Oh, dear! now I'm frighten'd out of my wits.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Don't you fear, I say; but come your ways home with me.

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: He will certainly challenge him!—

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Come, come, Phœbe,
odd rabbit it, I'll be up with him.—Come, follow me down to the inn yonder.

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: I will find some means to prevent their fighting. Well, I will return home, I will.

sp.speaker: First Wait.
sp.p: Mr. Humphrey, your master has been here, calling for you at a most furious rate.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Here! he must have made good haste to be here before me, tho' to be sure I came along rather soberly.

sp.speaker: First Wait.
sp.p: He swore terribly at you for making no haste at all.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: I never heard him swear an oath in my life!

sp.speaker: First Wait.
sp.p: Never heard him swear?—He call'd you all the names—

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Oh, I am us'd to that—It is only a way of speaking—he is never really angry.

sp.speaker: First Wait.
sp.p: “An idle rascal,” says he.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Did he call me so?
Ah, it meant nothing

sp.speaker: First Wait.
sp.p: “A loitering scoundrel—”

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: That's a hard word too,
but he meant nothing

sp.speaker: First Wait.
sp.p: Then he call'd you Renard, and said you were a Frenchman.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: What?—A Frenchman?—No, I won't be call'd a Frenchman, neither.—Do I look like a Frenchman.

sp.speaker: First Wait.
sp.p: No, I can't say you do; but he said you was one, and that you was always out of the way.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: He is a good deal more out of the way himself.

sp.speaker: First Wait.
sp.p: Here he comes.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: The more I think of this strange adventure, the more perplex'd I am.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: He is quite solid again.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: It must have been a stratagem of some jealous or malicious rival to prevent my success with Miss Milford.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: No symptoms of the fits, now.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: I'll write to Mr. Milford, and ask his permission to see him again.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: None at all—we are all right again.— How could that varlet tell me he was roaring and swearing! Folks tell such lies in these great towns! we shall do yet. That story of the little girl must have been part of his scheme to try Miss Emily's affection—It did not turn out well—that's natural enough, because he did not let me manage it for him. Miss Emily will do very well for us, and we'll take her down into the country directly.—We shall sit down, so quiet and comfortable there, after our journey—put the great arm chair by the hall door, and rest ourselves so nicely—so snug—
sp.stage: (draws a chair forward, and sits down)
sp.p: —so snug—so comfortable— all to ourselves.—

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Can you dance?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Dance!—Oh, I must give up the arm chair.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Aye, can you dance, my good fellow?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Now I believe he really thinks I am a Frenchman.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Allons! regardez moi!
Let us try a turn of the Spanish fandango.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Lord, Sir, I can't dance the fandangles, not I.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Come, commençez—balançez on one leg.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Balance on one leg! Zounds, I can hardly balance myself on two.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Odds, my life, there he is again! Oh, I have caught you, Squire, have I?

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Ah, Frank! how are you, my good fellow? Comment vat-il? how are you?
A plague! the sight of this fellow will bring his sister Phœbe into my head as much as ever. Go on, my friend.
You'll excuse me, Frank, while I just finish a pas de dance. Diable! why don't you dance?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Come, come, Squire, this won't do.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Won't it? I hope it will.—Come, step out.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Yes, Sir, I'll do that directly.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Where are you going?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: To step out, as you bid me.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: No, no, parbleu! I cannot part with you, now.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: You're full of your anticks, Squire, but I'm not so inclin'd to mirth; you've zet about poor Phœbe so, that you've e'en a'most broke the poor girl's heart.—Now, I've made up my mind about the matter, and so I wants to ask you a few questions of what you thinks best to be done in this case.—
sp.stage: [Peregrine expresses impatience, as if wishing to dance, tho' oblig'd to listen while Frank is speaking.]

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Il faut qu'elle danse—she must dance, my dear friend;—you see it is what I do myself—it is the only cure for a foolish passion.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE.—An apartment in Justice Touchit's House.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: WHO, do you say, want's me?

sp.speaker: Greg.
sp.p: A young woman, Sir.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Bid her come in.
Now, my young friend, what do you—Eh! how! what, my old friend's daughter, little Phœbe? my little rose-bud? What brings you here, my dear?— Here, come, and let me hear all you have to say—
sp.stage: (takes a chair, and seats her by him.)

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: Sir—I came, Sir—I had a great favour to beg, Sir—but I am so frighten'd—I don't know how to tell you what it is.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Come, come, let me hear.

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: I am afraid, Sir—that my brother— you must know, Sir—that there's a gentleman— a young gentleman, Sir—I'm so frighten'd, Sir —I'm afraid my brother will fight him.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: A duel! Oh, we'll easily put a stop to that —Here, Tippy!—
—do you go and look immediately for Mr. Frank Woodbine, who was here yesterday; and detain him on my warrant —He left his direction in the hall.
Now, my little girl, your heart may be at ease, now let me know what it is about, and who your brother is going to challenge.

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: Dear Sir—the story is—a gentleman came to our house, last autumn—

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Oh, say no more—I know the whole story. It is that gentleman with the odd name, from Cornwall, Mr.—Mr.—

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: Yes, Sir, Mr.—

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Single—Peregrine Single—that's an ugly story, my little rose-bud.—Can you answer for it, that he never did you any harm?

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: No, Sir, none in the world—only brother was so angry at the sight of him—you're quite sure they won't fight, Sir?

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: I tell you it cannot be;—what do you tremble for?

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: Only if they should, Sir—you know, if my brother should kill him—I mean if he should kill my poor brother, you know, Sir—

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Don't I tell you they cannot meet; and if they did, no harm comes of it now-a-days; these matters are settled in the pleasantest manner imaginable.

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: Indeed, Sir?

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Oh, yes—Well, but do you know where Mr. Peregrine is?

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: At the great inn, on the hill, Sir.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: I'll go myself to the inn with my officers, and bind the Squire over to the peace—I'll make a speech on the occasion.—In the mean time, three of my men shall be on the look out, that we may make sure of him, and you shall go with me, my little moss-rose. I am afraid that Peregrine is a very impudent fellow—“Eh, is not he?”

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: “Not that I know, Sir.”

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: “Edad, on recollection, I don't know whether I am not very angry with you, and whether I shall stand your friend or not.”

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: “Dear Sir! have pity on me!”

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: “This beating heart feels ev'ry fear, “That love and duty own; “Ah, Sir, preserve a life so dear, “Which you can save alone.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: “From course of law I may not swerve.

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: “A life so dear preserve!

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: “That look would melt a heart of stone. “So great a favour could you hope? “What, if he should deserve a rope!

sp.speaker: Phoe.
sp.p: “On you alone my hopes rely.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: “Don't ask me, fie!—

sp.speaker: Phoe.
sp.p: “Alas! I have no friend but you.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: “The law I keep in view.

sp.speaker: Phoe.
sp.p: “My hopes rely “On you alone.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: “Well, well, I'll try “What can be done.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: A pretty business I made of it, to be sure, at Mr. Milford's! a pleasant method of paying my addresses! Half my embarrassment arose from the stupidity of Humphrey. Where could he have got that strange letter? His discourse is so wild, lately, I begin to suspect his brain is a little gone.

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: Pray, Sir, is your name Single?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: It is, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: Then I have Justice Touchit's orders to detain you on his warrant.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Me, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: Till you give security for the peace with Frank Woodbine.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Woodbine! that is the name I heard something of this morning.

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: There's two more of our men upon the look out for you.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Well, Sir, I shall be glad of an opportunity of clearing my character. This is my room.

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: I'll see you into it, if you please, Sir.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: Enter Touchit, followed by Gregory and an Officer.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Gregory, walk more to the left! keep your hands straight! and, d'ye hear, don't sing. And you, Sir, don't you laugh! or if you do, let it be on the wrong side of your mouth.

sp.speaker: Greg.
sp.p: Lord, Sir, mayn't we—

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Peace, I say! I must teach these fellows to shew me proper respect. Hark'ye, damsel! Who's there?
Ah, my little Taffline, is it you?

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Yes, an please your worship, it is nobody but hurself at your worship's service.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Shew me the apartment of Peregrine Single, Esq.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Oh, hur couscience, how shall hur know all the apartments of the gentlemen who come here?— your worship knows in hur discretion, it is impossible.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Ah, you little rogue, I fancy—E'hem!— right, Taffline!—in discretion, the less you know of the gentlemen's apartments, the better.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Hush, your worship! there is a gentleman on the stairs now—perhaps, this is the gentleman.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Varlets, proceed! Are Tippy, Cramp, and Pinch gone, as I order'd?—Speak out.

sp.speaker: Greg.
sp.p: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Very well, go on—I shall find the room, I warrant.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Hur does now know if the gentleman is that name or not, but hur will not let him be taken away because he has promised hur a cap and sash. Hur will try to get the monies before he goes, and buy them hurself.

sp.speaker: Tippy.
sp.p: Well, Cramp, I've found him.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.p: You found him! where did you find him?

sp.speaker: Tip.
sp.p: Just at the back gate of the inn.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.p: How can that be, man? I found him myself.

sp.speaker: Tip.
sp.p: What! Mr. Single?

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.p: Ay, surely, I found him at the front gate.

sp.speaker: Tip.
sp.p: How can you say so?

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.p: How can you say otherwise?

sp.speaker: Tip.
sp.p: Here's Pinch; he shall see if I have not got him.

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: Well, my lads, he's found.

sp.speaker: Cra. & Tip.
sp.p: Yes, yes, I've found him.

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: You found him! why, I found him.

sp.speaker: Cra. & Tip.
sp.p: You!

sp.speaker: Tip.
sp.p: What, is he the devil then, in three places, at once?

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: I tell you I've got him yonder in his room. Where's the Justice?

sp.speaker: Tip.
sp.p: I heard his voice, and came to look for him.

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: Bring in your men, and let's see them.— A couple of blockheads!

div.head: Scene
div.stage: Enter Peregrine, led by Cramp and another Officer.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Peste! au diable! don't tell me, fellow, of challenges and securities;—I believe this town is inhabited by lunatics.—I should by this time have paid seven or eight visits, have taken a lesson at small sword, sparr'd, rode, and danc'd.—I'll punish you, you rascals, for hindering a gentleman's improvements in this manner.—But who comes here?—Oh, here comes the Justice, I suppose.—Egad, this will be be a trying scene.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Hem! Is your name, Single, Sir?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Yes, that's he, Sir—don't ask him many questions, your worship, because they make him wild.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Est il possible!—What brings my pretty Phœbe hither?

sp.speaker: Phoe.
sp.p: I could not believe you had left me willingly, and determin'd to follow you, to know what could induce you to forsake me.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Now, a plague of it, I am sorry she loves me so much—I 'faith, my dear girl, you know I always told you, constancy was a tedious virtue, mere ennui—therefore, ha! ha! three capers and off.— Diable! I wish I could cast off this couple.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Mad! why he's more merry than mad.—I should like to crack a bottle with him:—but—hem!—I must bind him over to the peace.

sp.speaker: Phoe
sp.p: I thought you were in earnest,
when you talk'd so to me.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: I cannot bear her tears.

sp.speaker: Phoe.
sp.p: You know you said I should be your wife.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Lord! that my master should tell such abominable—It's all a tham, Sir.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Don't tell me of shams—I'll make him give a good reason, or a good portion, for breaking his word with her.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Pray, Sir, who are you?

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: I am a magistrate, Sir, and demand of you, —what is the meaning of all this, Sir?—This fellow will make me laugh, and spoil all my dignity as a magistrate.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Go on, Sir; you are a magistrate, and demand of me—

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Zounds! can I talk to you while you are dancing? I shall long to cut a caper myself, presently

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: I must dance, while that young lady is in the room! I have nothing else left for it.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Step down, my dear, and if they have found your brother, let me know.
Now, Sir, can you hear me quietly? Can you stand still now?

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: If you please, Sir.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Sir, I demand of you a proper security for your keeping the peace with Frank Woodbine, a brother of that girl.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: De tout mon cœur, old gentleman—I have not the least desire to fight for nothing.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: How, Sir! E'hem!—Do you call it nothing to seduce the affections of a poor unsuspecting girl, and then leave her to wretchedness, while you are diverting yourself with the simplicity of the next you meet, as innocent as she was, and whom you will render as miserable as she is!—
There's a speech for a country magistrate—what a figure I should make upon the bench!

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Oh, hur was afraid so—the Justice has cot him, but hur has not cot her cap and sash— hur must get it—Ah, sweet, cruel, prave gentleman, how can you pear to leave hur after all your fair promises?

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: How's this? another!—why you are as licentious as the grand Turk.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: What, the diable, is the matter now?—who are you pray?
“This is the little woman as I've heard tell,” &c.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Ah, you pretend not to know hur now! Oh, fie for shame! cannot you pear hur witness in your own conscience?

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: What, did you promise to marry her too?

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Peste, diantre! Sir, do you think I can marry all woman kind?—if you have nothing more to say to me, Sir, I shall if you please—

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Hold, hold, Sir! there are farther reasons for not setting you yet at your liberty.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Don't let my master go, Sir—keep us at home, if you please, your worship! That we should be exposed so before the Justice!

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Hark'ye, honest fellow, a word with you;
Do you retire to your room, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Well, Sir, I suppose I must go, because I cannot resist; but it is diablement hard to lose the public breakfast at the long room, and the fete champetre, besides a turn to the Wells, with some of the prettiest girls in Christendom!

sp.speaker: Touch
sp.p: He's a very devil after the girls. Step down stairs, Taffline, for the present.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Oh, hur has lost her cap and swash.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Come, hither, my friend. How long have you observ'd this change of which you was telling me in your master's behaviour?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Never, till we came here, Sir, any way in the world. He was the most orderly young gentleman —nobody could have a better character than we had all over the country. Don't you think, your worship, that my master must be crazy?

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Crazy? certainly.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: I am glad to hear your worship say so, Mr. Justice—I did not know very well which of us it was; but as it is he, poor gentleman, I'll go and comfort him.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Do so.

sp.speaker: Tip.
sp.p: We have found Mr. Single, Sir; would you have him brought in here?

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Brought here! why he is here already.

sp.speaker: Tip.
sp.p: Oh, aye, here he is—I bid him wait.

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: La! you must ask uncle—I cannot tell you.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Why how did he get out of his room again? Where did you find him?

sp.speaker: Tip.
sp.p: Just at the back gate of the hotel; he answers the description, and so I brought him, though he will give no account of himself.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: Arrah, and how can you expect a poor simpleton like this to give an account of himself, of whom nature has given so little account?
What do you look at him for? can't you see without looking, that his wit may stand in a nutshell?

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: I want to see Taffline.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: And just now he would not know her!— he's certainly crazy.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: Come along, my dear boy, and to-morrow, we'll set off upon our journey. There's no keeping him still for half a day in the same place, if I am not always carrying him about from town to town.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Do you stand there, that he may not get out again. Into the Moon! perhaps he may find his wits there.
Where do you come from?

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: I found the gentleman, Sir, directly, and have kept him waiting some time for your further orders.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: You found him! where did you find him?

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: Just here, Sir, by the front gate.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: The back gate, you mean.

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: No, Sir, the front.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Why, here's some mistake; you've mistaken your man.

sp.speaker: Pinch
sp.p: No, no, there's no mistake.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Do you dare to contradict me, Sirrah?— I tell you there is a mistake.—Tippy found him at the back gate of the hotel, and you pretend—

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: Then I'm sure the gentleman may prove an alibi.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: An alibi!

how the devil came it into your head to think of his proving an alibi?—I won't be angry with you for that. Bring out the person you have in custody—I'll apologize to him for your blunder, and dismiss him.

This is always the case! always troubled to mend the blunders of these ignorant fellows! If he be a gentleman, and comprehend a good speech when he hears it, I shall have another opportunity of making a figure on the occasion.

div.stage: Enter Pertinax, Pinch, and Humphrey, from the Hydra.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: It is by your orders, I presume, Sir—

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Why he is here! How the devil came you in at the front gate, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Sir?—

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: How came you there, Sir?—Why, I saw you go into the Moon just now!

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Lord. Sir! d'ye take my master for the man in the moon?
He's quite quiet, now, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Your officer will inform you, Sir, I have been in my own room, here, this half hour, in obedience to your warrant.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: What! half an hour?—Why, you was here just now, dancing and capering, that the Devil could not hold you still.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Your officer will answer that.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: And were you not here again this minute with your uncle?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Sir, I am really at a loss to comprehend you; your officer will answer you.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: In the name of wonder, who are you?— What is your name?

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Single.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: No, e'cod, you're not Single; I'll swear; you're double, if not treble. Single!—Single!

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Pertinax Single, of Cornwall.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Pertinax! Pertinax Single!—Ha! ha! I smell a rat. Stay here a moment; stay a moment.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: This is the strangest conduct—

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Yes, Sir; we seem all in a strange way.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Do you know this magistrate, Humphrey?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Surely, Sir, I don't know that I know any body any way in the world.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: What a great thing to be a magistrate! Never saw any thing like it! I am really afraid, Sir, there has been a little mistake.
You may go now about your business. I shan't have any further occasion for you.
If I could persuade your brother to come out,—

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: My brother!
sp.stage: (goes to the Door of the Moon)
sp.p: It is he, indeed! 'tis my brother Percival!
Ha! Percival! my dear brother!

sp.speaker: Perc.
sp.p: Oh, dear! brother Perty! La! I'm glad you're come.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Oh, lud! it was my master's brother, after all. Odd, hang it! I'm so glad! What! is it he that is abroad, Sir?

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Abroad! your wit is abroad, instead of your master's. I tell you he is here.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: And we did not expect him home this twelvemonth. My life on't, that's what has made so many mistakes.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Mistakes! yes; I don't wonder at that. Nobody but a justice could have found it out so cleverly in a minute
sp.stage: (goes to the Door of the Moon, half opens it, and looks into the Room)
sp.p: Yes, yes, there they are, both together.
I can- guess, my poor fellow, how you can distinguish.—
sp.stage: (Peregrine opens the window of the Daffodil)
sp.p: —Oh, Lord! oh, Lord! here, too!

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Pray, Sir, how long am I to be confin'd in this room?

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: In that room! why, you are not in that room; you are both in the other room.

sp.speaker: Pereg.
sp.p: Am I at liberty to go to the Wells yet?

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Is not this your master, Humphrey?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: To be sure it is, Sir.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Ha! ha! I have it again—a great thing to be a justice.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: My life on't, we have got all three here.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: The unimproved state in which I still find my younger brother, is no small abatement of the pleasure such an agreeable surprise would otherwise have occasion'd me.

sp.speaker: Touch
sp.p: Now, egad, I'll give him another agreeable surprise.—Do me the favour, Sir, to walk into this room.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Into that room, Sir? I seem to have nothing to do but to go into rooms; but, as you request it, Sir,—

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Odds heart! yonder comes Frank with his sister!—Eh! who is that lady with her?

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Lud! that is the very lady, I told you, Mr. Justice, we were going to be married to—if it had not been for an unlucky letter; by which it seemed as if we had been courting another woman, of the name of Phœbe Woodbine.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Ah! ah! very good, very good, indeed!

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Very good!—no; 'twas very bad, Sir! for miss Milford's father was so angry, he won't see us again.

div.stage: Enter Emily, Phoebe, Taffline, and Frank.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Ah, my little rose-bud! zounds, that a fellow should be such a fool, to prefer his hops and jumps, and French cotillions, to a nice little bit of stuff of true English petticoat!

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Well, measter Touchit, what if it be a stuff petticoat?—We may be as honest and as good gentlefolk, too, as those that flaunts about in their silks. The more we saves in those things, the more we has for the poor.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Aye, Frank; and may every honest warm hearted fellow, like yourself, who has cheerfully shared the burthens of the poor in a winter of scarcity, be rewarded with a plentiful harvest!—there, that's one of the best speeches I ever made in my life!

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Our Phœbe won't ha' the 'Squire now.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Ah! why so?

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: Because, Sir, he has given away his heart to this lady.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha! that's very good.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: Some circumstances, Phœbe, make me doubtful of Mr. Single's heart; but, however I might excuse those, I can no longer have any thoughts of his hand, since I find the libertine offers he has made to this servant.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha! very good again.

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: And hur is sure it is creat shame if a prave gentleman, like Mr. Shingles, is not made hur some handsome gifts for taking such creat liperties with her.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Oh, excellent! excellent!

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: This may be a woundy good joke; but—

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: And creat shame the chudge should laugh, too.

sp.speaker: Vouch.
sp.p: Hem! that's true; I forget my gravity as a magistrate.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: This unexpected meeting, Sir, with my two brothrs,—Miss Milford!—

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: Mr. Pertinax!

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: Peregrine!

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: Cot pless her, Mr. Perceval!

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Hold your tongues, you foolish girls! Hem! Some mistakes, I understand, Sir, have arisen between you and this young lady,
which will all be clear'd up when she hears what I now tell her; that your two brothers are likewise in this inn, and that you are all so alike, that none but a justice can know one from the other.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: I thank you, Sir, for saving me an explanation.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Be so good, Sir, to desire your brother, yonder,
to walk out.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Excuse my brother Percival, Sir; but, if you will give me leave to set Peregrine at liberty,—

sp.speaker: Phœ.
sp.p: Peregrine! why you are Peregrine!

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.p: No, no; Pertinax!

sp.speaker: Taff.
sp.p: No; hur is Mr. Percival.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Hold your tongues, I say:—your brother Peregrine's liberty is in your power, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: Then I'll set him free directly.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: Hold! hold! Sir, on this condition —that you first persuade him to make good his word to this young girl, whose affections he has stolen. Till you bring me your word for that, I insist on his not stirring.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
Humph.
sp.p: Now, do, Ma'am; do you go with us to our papa's, and let him know all about these mistakes. I told you, ma'am, that our character was a very excellent one.

sp.speaker: Pertin.
sp.p: I will then immediately return; and, if this pretty girl is content, persuade my brother to be as happy a man as myself.

sp.speaker: Touch.
sp.p: And I'll dance at both your weddings— Egad, we'll have a merry party—We'll invite all present.

sp.speaker: Phoebe.
sp.p: Oh! happy me, whose fears now past, The present joy enhance!

sp.speaker: Peregrine,
sp.stage: at the window of the Daffodil.
sp.p: Ha! Ha! A pas de deux at last! Let Hymen lead the dance.

sp.speaker: Humphrey.
sp.p: Since, truly, we must married be, What says my pretty maid?

sp.speaker: Taffline.
sp.p: If truly hur your heart could see, Hur would not be afraid.

sp.speaker: Percival
sp.stage: at the Window of the Moon.
sp.p: Now, Uncky, mayn't I take a peep? I heard my sweet Taffline—

sp.speaker: Mac Floggen.
sp.p: Be still, be still, you silly sheep; Your talking will be seen.

sp.speaker: Humphrey and Frank.
sp.p: The case is clear, the wonder o'er.

sp.speaker: Touchit.
sp.p: My wisdom here is plain—

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Sure never met such three before, And may not meet again.

sp.stage: (During the last line, Pertinax returns with Mr. Milford and Emily.—Pertinax advances to the audience.)
sp.p: My pride in your indulgence be— My will be my excuse— I hope, while here I play the Three, You will not play the Deuce.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Our task is done, and all is said; Our will be our excuse! We trust, if well the Three be play'd, We need not fear the Deuce.
